intro: Glastonbury already draws pilgrims for its abbey and its legends, and one more waits in the churchyard of St John the Baptist. The Glastonbury Thorn is a hawthorn that flowers twice a year, once with everything else in spring and once around midwinter, when nothing else in England is doing much of anything. Every specimen descends from grafted cuttings tied to a legend of Joseph of Arimathea. Since 1929 a flowering sprig has been cut each December and sent to the reigning monarch, a tradition this particular tree still keeps.
meta_description: The Glastonbury Thorn flowers twice a year and supplies the monarch's Christmas sprig every December, a tradition kept since 1929. Free, in the churchyard.
question_meta: The Glastonbury Thorn in St John's churchyard flowers twice a year and supplies the monarch's Christmas sprig. Where to find it, and its ninety-year story.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Glastonbury is the Glastonbury Thorn, a hawthorn in the churchyard of St John the Baptist on the High Street. It was planted in the 1930s by George Chislett, then head gardener of Glastonbury Abbey, which makes it about ninety years old. It flowers twice a year, and every December a flowering sprig is cut by pupils of St John's Infants School and sent to the reigning monarch, a tradition kept since 1929. It is free to visit, standing in the churchyard, open in daylight hours.
question_context: This is the tree that lasted, not the first one. Tradition says the whole Glastonbury Thorn lineage descends from a staff planted by Joseph of Arimathea, a story first written down in 1520, and a Parliamentary soldier is said to have cut down the original around 1647. Every specimen since has been grafted, because the twice-flowering trait does not survive from seed. Glastonbury has lost two others: the tree on Wearyall Hill was vandalised in 2010, its replacement sapling snapped in 2012, and the whole tree was removed by the landowner in 2019; the specimen inside Glastonbury Abbey died in 1991 and was felled the following year. This one, grafted by Abbey head gardener George Chislett in the 1930s, is what remains. It has not had an easy run either: a 2018 report called it decrepit and heavily infested with mistletoe, though a December 2024 visit found it much healthier and flowering well. The coordinates given are the church's rather than a tree-level pin, so the location is marked approximate until someone has stood in the churchyard and confirmed exactly where in it the tree grows.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Glastonbury?
faq.a: The Glastonbury Thorn, a hawthorn in the churchyard of St John the Baptist, planted in the 1930s and roughly ninety years old.

faq.q: Why does it flower twice a year?
faq.a: It is Crataegus monogyna 'Biflora', a hawthorn variety that flowers once in spring like any other and again around midwinter. The trait only survives by grafting, so every Holy Thorn in Glastonbury is a cutting of the last one.

faq.q: Why is a sprig cut from it every December?
faq.a: Since 1929, pupils from St John's Infants School have cut a flowering sprig each December and sent it to the reigning monarch, a tradition that continues today.
Yes. It stands in the churchyard of St John the Baptist on the High Street, open to the public in daylight hours.

trees.name: The Glastonbury Thorn

location.address: Churchyard of the Church of St John the Baptist, High Street, Glastonbury, Somerset, BA6 9DR

trees.story:
Every December, children from St John's Infants School cut a flowering sprig from this hawthorn and send it to the reigning monarch. They have done it since 1929. The tree can oblige because it is Crataegus monogyna 'Biflora', a hawthorn that flowers twice a year, once in spring like every other one and once around midwinter, when nothing else in the churchyard is doing anything at all. The trait does not survive seed, so every Holy Thorn in Glastonbury is a cutting grafted from the last one.

This specimen was planted in the 1930s by George Chislett, then head gardener at Glastonbury Abbey, who learned to graft Holy Thorn cuttings onto blackthorn rootstock. That makes it about ninety years old, and it is the one that lasted. The Abbey's tree died in 1991 and was cut down the following year. The tree on Wearyall Hill was attacked in December 2010, lost its replacement sapling in 2012, and was taken out altogether in 2019.

By tradition the whole lineage descends from a staff pushed into the ground by Joseph of Arimathea, a story first written down in 1520, and a Parliamentary soldier is said to have felled the original around 1647. Recent decades have been harder on it than any legend. In 2018 it was described as decrepit and heavily infested with mistletoe. A visit in December 2024 found it almost clear of the stuff and flowering well.
trees.access: Free. Standing in the churchyard of St John the Baptist, open to the public in daylight hours, right on Glastonbury's High Street.
trees.transport: No railway station in Glastonbury; nearest is Castle Cary, about 11 miles away. Frequent local bus services stop in the town centre, about 5 minutes' walk from the churchyard.

best_time.label: December, when the winter flowering comes and the Christmas sprig is cut

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by when it flowers, around midwinter as well as in spring, when nothing else in the churchyard is doing anything at all. It stands in the churchyard of St John the Baptist on the High Street.

location_site.name: Churchyard of St John the Baptist, High Street

trees.name: Magog, the Surviving Oak of Gog and Magog

location.address: Edge of Wick Farm, eastern foot of Glastonbury Tor, near Stone Down Lane, Glastonbury

trees.access: Free to see. The oaks stand at the edge of Wick Farm beside the lane and footpath below Stone Down, at the eastern foot of Glastonbury Tor. They are on farmland, so view them from the path and do not go into the fields.
trees.transport: No railway station in Glastonbury; local bus to the town centre, then roughly 40 to 50 minutes' walk east past the foot of the Tor (about 2.5 km)
trees.story:
Gog is dead, and Magog is hanging on. The two oaks at the foot of Stone Down, east of Glastonbury Tor, are the last of an ancient avenue or grove of oaks that once stood here. In 1906 the rest were felled to make farmland. One of the felled trees was reported at the time to be eleven feet across with more than 2,000 rings, a figure nobody can check now that the wood is gone.

The two that were spared carry the names of the legendary giants Gog and Magog, though even the Glastonbury Conservation Society admits nobody is sure which is which. What it can say is that the tree on the right, if you stand with the Tor behind you, still comes into green leaf every spring. Thirty years ago, the Society notes, the other oak looked much the healthier of the two. Now it is dead, its remains scarred by an accidental candle fire in April 2017, and the Woodland Trust's writer called the living one close to the end of her life in 2024.

How old Magog is, nobody knows. Popular accounts range from about a thousand years to more than two thousand. No girth has been published and no one has dated the living tree, so we leave the age open. If you have measured it, tell us.

The pair stand on farmland at the edge of Wick Farm. They are seen from the lane and footpath beside them.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the living one of the pair, the oak on the right when you stand with the Tor behind you; its partner is a dead, fire-scarred hulk. They stand at the edge of Wick Farm below Stone Down.

trees.name: The Yews of Chalice Well

location.address: Chalice Well Gardens, 85-89 Chilkwell Street, Glastonbury BA6 8DD

trees.access: Paid entry to Chalice Well Gardens (run by the Chalice Well Trust, open to visitors; current hours and prices on chalicewell.org.uk, site not fetched)
trees.transport: No railway station in Glastonbury; local bus to the High Street, then about 15 minutes' walk along Chilkwell Street

location_site.name: Chalice Well Gardens, south end near the Holy Thorn

trees.story:
In 1961, digging beneath Chalice Well, excavators found the stump of a yew still in the ground where it had grown. Professor R.D. Preston of Leeds dated it to early Roman times, around 300 AD. The Ancient Yew Group, which records Britain's old yews, suggests it may have been an ancestor of the yews that grow beside the well today. That stump is long dead, and it says nothing about the age of the living trees. It does show that a yew grew at this spring in Roman Britain.

The living yews are harder to pin down. The largest are a pair of male yews at the south end of the garden, near the Holy Thorn, which the Yew Group measured in 2006 at between eight and ten feet round. No one has published an age for them. If you know more, tell us.

The garden's most photographed yew is a different tree. It splits into two stems close to the ground and joins up again at about six feet, leaving an opening between, and it goes by the name of the Yoni tree, after a female symbol, although the Yew Group points out that the tree itself is male. On the eastern edge of the garden stands another old yew whose two trunks have grown back together.

Chalice Well is a garden around a spring at the foot of Chalice Hill, run by the Chalice Well Trust, with paid entry.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise the pair as the largest yews in the garden, two male trees 8 to 10 feet round. They stand at the south end of Chalice Well Gardens near the Holy Thorn; the yew that splits low and rejoins is a different tree.
